title: Climate migration
subtitle: 216 million displaced by 2050?
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: The climate will force hundreds of millions of people to leave home, and no international law protects them yet.

hero.hook: The climate already drives out more people than war, and no law knows what to call them.

blocks.text: Rising water does not always arrive as a spectacular wave. It nibbles away a field first, then a well, then a whole village. Elsewhere, extreme heat makes the air almost impossible to breathe. In both cases entire families have to leave, not because of a war but because of the climate. These forced departures have a name: **climate migration**. The problem is that no international law really recognizes them.

sections.title: An exodus already bigger than war

blocks.text: In **2022**, one figure marked a turning point: climate disasters caused **60 million internal displacements**, forced departures inside a single country. For the first time, that number passed the number of people fleeing wars.

In **2009**, the government of the Maldives, one of the [[Low-lying island states]], held a cabinet meeting underwater, in scuba gear and oxygen tanks, to warn the world that the archipelago could disappear.

blocks.caption: Migrants crossing the Mediterranean: the climate crisis now joins political crises as a driver of departure

blocks.text: What comes next looks more worrying. The **World Bank** estimates that without a massive effort, climate change could force **216 million people** to migrate by **2050**. In Bangladesh, the ocean is eating farmland. In sub-Saharan Africa, water is running short. In the Pacific, some island states risk losing their territory completely.

sections.title: Two speeds of rupture: the shock and the slow grind

blocks.text: The climate drives people out in two ways. **Sudden disasters**, like storms, cause abrupt departures that are often temporary, until they repeat so often that people lose the strength to bounce back. **Slow degradation** changes a place forever: rising water makes the soil salty, killing crops long before the sea reaches the houses, while desertification turns pasture into barren land bit by bit, pushing nomadic communities toward [[forced settlement]] or exile to the cities.

A new threat worries scientists: **humid heat**. When temperature and humidity pass a certain threshold, the body can no longer cool itself by sweating. By 2050, parts of the Persian Gulf and South Asia could become deadly for anyone who stays outside more than a few hours.

sections.title: A legal vacuum facing a global crisis

blocks.text: Despite the obvious crisis, people displaced by the climate fall into the [[legal vacuum of the "climate refugee"]]. The phrase is everywhere in the media, but it carries no weight in international law: the Geneva Convention of 1951 protects people persecuted by their own state, but climate change is nobody's specific fault. It is a global phenomenon.

With no official status, these people are not covered by the principle of **[[non-refoulement]]**, which forbids sending someone back to a place where their life would be in danger. That gap creates an injustice: the hardest-hit countries have historically polluted least, while rich countries often close their borders. Hence the idea of a **climate debt**, the moral responsibility of industrialized countries toward the people made vulnerable by their own development.

Some countries are already looking for new answers. Small island states are studying how to remain a nation recognized by the UN even if their island vanishes under water. Kiribati, for example, has bought land in Fiji to prepare, if needed, the relocation of its whole population.

In 2018, the **Global Compact for Migration** began to mention the environmental causes of departure. But the priority is still **local adaptation**: sea walls, salt-resistant crops, warning systems, so that people can stay home as long as possible. Migration you did not choose is always felt as a failure, and massive, disorderly flows risk feeding tensions over water and livable land.

In 2022, climate disasters caused 60 million internal displacements, passing war refugees for the first time. With no recognized legal status, these people have no protection against a crisis that could affect 216 million people by 2050.
